 What we know
 • Death toll rises: More bodies have been pulled from the rubble of a New York building collapse that killed at least eight people , according to fire officials. At least 19 people, including firefighters and children , were injured after the three-story structure fell yesterday afternoon. Rescue workers don’t know how many people may still be trapped.
 • Perilous rescues: Showers have begun at the collapse site in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood, with potential for soaking rain this afternoon that could further complicate an “extremely dangerous” rescue operation. Firefighters have pulled people from a mountain of debris, placing them on stretchers and carrying them up ladders .
 • Cause unknown: Investigators are looking into what caused the building to collapse into an adjacent construction site, trapping people in both. Officials are concerned about a secondary structural fall .

 First round of rain approaching building collapse site
 By Meteorologist Mary Gilbert 
 A quick-moving batch of showers is tracking north along the New Jersey shore and will soon reach parts of Brooklyn.
 Rain is likely to arrive around 11 a.m. ET and will be brief, but could be enough to wet the ground and muddy up some of the site.
 Any shower chances will be spotty after this first batch moves through until steadier rain arrives later this afternoon.
 The best chance for more of a soaking rain is still within 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. ET. Brooklyn could see rain on and off through much of Friday, with dry breaks possible in between batches of showers.

 Mayor Mamdani to speak at noon briefing on building collapse
 By Andy Rose 
 Debris is seen at the Brooklyn building collapse site on Thursday morning. 
 FDNY 
 New York fire officials and Mayor Zohran Mamdani will hold a news conference at noon Thursday about the deadly building collapse in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn.
 The news conference will take place near the site of the collapse, the mayor’s office said.
 Eight people are confirmed dead after firefighters spent the night searching through rubble looking for people buried underneath. Another four victims are in critical condition, the Fire Department of the City of New York said.
 Mamdani spoke at a briefing yesterday, saying he was “ heartbroken ” by the loss of life.

 Residents formed prayer circle for woman who lost husband in Brooklyn building collapse 
 0:39
 As she heard the wailing of a young woman who lost her spouse in the collapse, Flatbush resident Joy Kerr led a prayer circle to offer some comfort in a moment of devastation.
 Kerr walked into a church near the site of the collapse and found the young woman crying hysterically after learning that her spouse, a construction worker, was killed when the building came down.
 Kerr listened to the woman sobbing for about half an hour and said, “No, I can’t take this. I can’t sit back and just watch her and listen to her cry so hysterically.”
 “In that moment, I knew she needed comfort,” she said.
 She gathered with the woman who had lost her spouse and those around them, and they began to pray.
 “This is devastating,” Kerr said of the collapse. “Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood, and we just need to come together and stay together as a community.”

 A widow wails her husband’s name after his body was pulled from the rubble
 By Brynn Gingras , Jeff Winter and Holly Yan 
 At Bethesda Church of God in Christ, the agonizing cries of a woman who just lost her husband reverberated through the Brooklyn sanctuary.
 The church, also called La Piscine de Bethesda, turned into an epicenter of anguish and anxiety Thursday as loved ones gathered to await information about those who may have been trapped in the nearby building collapse.
 When the woman learned her husband’s body was pulled from the debris Thursday morning, she collapsed and wailed her husband’s name:
 “Tomás! Tomasito!” she cried.
 Family members gathered around the widow and started a prayer circle.
 Just outside the church, a nervous father also prayed. He was anxiously waiting to learn the fate of his son, a construction worker who has not been reachable since the collapse.

 Flatbush's “Little Caribbean” is a hub of the Afro-Caribbean community
 By Rebekah Riess 
 Wednesday’s deadly residential building collapse happened in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood, “a dynamic and culturally diverse community,” known as “Little Caribbean” and “Little Haiti,” according to NYC Small Business Services.
 With a population of over 200,000, the area is both economically and culturally diverse. African Americans make up 71 percent of residents, and the Hispanic or Latinx population makes up 12 percent, according to city data .
 Thirty percent of the population speaks a language other than English at home, most commonly Haitian Creole, Spanish, and Arabic, according to the city.
 “Little Caribbean is a place where … people, restaurants, and small businesses come together to share social and cultural histories, living legacies, and futures,” the neighborhood’s website says , adding that the neighborhood “celebrates the rich history of the Caribbean Diaspora in New York City.”

 Resident describes scene in Brooklyn after building collapsed 
 0:31
 Katie Stevens, a teacher who lives about a block from the three-story building that collapsed in Flatbush on Wednesday watched a terrifying scene play out in the hours after the building came down.
 Stevens was home from work for Veteran’s Day when she heard the collapse, at first mistaking the sound for construction that had been ongoing in the area. When she walked down the block to investigate, she saw a man, woman and child holding each other and crying.
 “The whole building next to ours just disappeared,” they told her.
 They had been evacuated from a neighboring building, and told her there were “so many children” in the building that collapsed, describing the families that lived there.
 Stevens heard people yelling for help from within the rubble Wednesday evening, followed by the sounds of firefighters cutting through metal to try to get to them.
 The teacher watched as firefighters rescued multiple people, a few who were transported away on stretchers.
 As the response continued this morning, she watched responders load body bags into a van.
 “I care for my neighbors so much,” Stevens told CNN. “I’m just so sad.”

 Department of Buildings, law enforcement jointly investigating fatal collapse
 By Gloria Pazmino 
 Emergency personnel work at the scene of a building collapse in the Brooklyn borough of New York on Wednesday. 
 Angelina Katsanis/Reuters 
 Dozens of Department of Buildings workers are back at the scene of a fatal collapse in the Flatbush section of Brooklyn Thursday as the agency continues an investigation to determine why a residential building collapsed into a construction site next door.
 The department is conducting the investigation alongside law enforcement, according to a department official with knowledge of the investigation.
 Department of Buildings inspectors and engineers are on site at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, the building that collapsed into an adjacent construction site Wednesday afternoon.
 Officials are also assisting first responders with recovery efforts and conducting structural stability inspections of other buildings in the immediate area, a department official told CNN.
 Officials have not yet determined the cause of the collapse, but for now they are zeroing in on records and site conditions at the collapsed building and the construction site where active excavation had been taking place prior to Wednesday’s collapse.
 Developers at the construction site located at 2625 Bedford Avenue had a permit for excavation and foundation work as part of a project to build a mixed-use residential apartment building, the official said.
 CNN has reached out to the developer.
 Seven months ago, the developers at the construction site were fined by the city for conducting demolition work without the proper permit and protections, including a lack of overhead protection such as sheds and netting for adjacent properties.
 Despite a stop-work order and a fine, the developers continued to work and demolish, resulting in a second fine by the Department of Buildings.
 As of May, the developers had cleared their violations and were back in good standing with regulating agencies, allowing construction to resume.
 Officials are now in the early stages of the investigation and it’s not yet clear whether the prior demolition work is directly related to Wednesday’s collapse. All permits for work at the site have been suspended.

 Water shut off to multiple buildings surrounding collapse site
 By Gloria Pazmino 
 About 100 buildings surrounding the rubble of the collapsed building in Flatbush, a central Brooklyn neighborhood, are currently without water, according to the New York City Department of Environmental Protection.
 “DEP has shut down city water mains so emergency crews can continue search and rescue operations,” an NYC Water post says.

 NYC has launched an investigation into how the building collapsed
 By Chris Boyette and Gloria Pazmino 
 Members of the FDNY work at the site of the building collapse in Brooklyn on Thursday. 
 Yuki Iwamura/AP 
 The New York City Department of Buildings has launched an investigation into what might have caused the deadly building collapse in Brooklyn Wednesday, and what, if any, warning signs may have been missed, Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said.
 “We will be looking into all aspects of the building and the neighboring construction site,” Tigani said .
 The chair of the City Council’s subcommittee on zoning and franchises, Farah N. Louis, called Thursday for an investigation by “all relevant municipal oversight agencies” into the building’s history of compliance with city safety, building, and housing laws.
 “What happened on Wednesday is completely unacceptable and raises serious questions that our community deserves clear answers to,” Louis said. “A building does not simply collapse in the middle of a residential neighborhood without warning signs or systemic failures.”
 Department of Building inspectors are at the scene of the collapse and have been all night, according to Tigani.

 Search dogs are at work on scene
 By Lauren Mascarenhas and Jeff Winter 
 WCBS 
 Search dogs are making their way through the rubble where the three-story building collapsed, as crews race to look for people who may be trapped under the debris before a storm moves into the area.
 The New York City Police Department’s Emergency Services Unit has deployed the canines, whose discerning noses and agile bodies may be able to help cover areas that officers cannot.
 The field of debris they are searching is now a pile of broken walls, bricks and bent beams. Clothes and insulation litter the piles of rubble that used to be the apartment building.

 Excavators clearing debris on scene of building collapse
 By Sara Smart and Jeff Winter 
 News 12 Brooklyn 
 Excavators moved into the building collapse site just before 8 a.m. Thursday.
 Two such heavy machines worked to clear debris, video shows, transferring it piecemeal onto Flatbush Avenue to be searched by hand and by dogs.

 Collapse very likely to have been caused by construction next door, says forensic engineer
 By Rebekah Riess 
 As images of the three-story structure collapse in Brooklyn emerge, forensic engineer Dan Eschenasy said it is very likely the collapse was caused by the adjacent construction site.
 The frame building with masonry walls and wood floors, on its own lacked structural support due to the presence of a store entrance with large windows instead of masonry at the street level, Eschenasy said.
 Removing the adjacent building essentially made the building a corner building, the retired Chief Structural Engineer of the NYC Department of Buildings said. Corner buildings with stores at their base are “extremely fragile,” he said.
 When excavation is done on an adjacent building, contractors are obliged by New York City Building Code to examine the capacity of the adjoining building when calculating construction loads, Eschenasy said.
 “A slight problem with supporting the excavation might have led to the collapse,” he explained. “Any movement beyond half an inch of the soil can start a collapse.”
 While this type of building may have had some fragilities due to age, not all old buildings next to construction sites collapse, he said. “The building code says you have to protect the adjacent building. It’s very clear. It’s an obligation,” Eschenasy said.
 The number of fatalities caused by the collapse is unusual, Eschenasy said. Typically, he said, “people hear some noises and they have the time to run out (…) they have like three four minutes to get out.”
 He believes the darkness may have had an impact on the fatality rate. “The firemen had problems understanding fully what was happening. They are extremely trained … They know what to do and they did whatever they could,” he said, adding there is a class they take on the collapse of masonry buildings.
 Eschenasy urged the public not to judge the Department of Buildings by this collapse, saying overall, these types of collapses have statistically decreased. “The code has become extremely, extremely strong, extremely demanding.” he said.
 Read more 
 Published Nov 12, 2026, 8:29 AM ET 
 Link Copied!
 Collapsed building was nearly a century old
 By Andy Rose 
 The building that collapsed Wednesday – 1321 Flatbush Avenue – had been part of its colorful neighborhood, now known as Little Haiti and Little Caribbean, for nearly a century.
 City records say the walkup, built in 1930, was permitted for four family residential units on its second and third floors, spread across 2,050 square feet, with a ground floor storefront and a storage cellar.
 It was not immediately clear how many apartments were occupied at the time of the collapse. The certificate of occupancy indicates it last had significant renovation in 1960.
 Photos of the building in the city’s property records show the business most recently occupying the building advertised a variety of services on its storefront sign, including medical uniforms and money transfers. Before its current business tenant, the commercial space had a “For Rent” sign hanging in front of it for five years. A partially faded signpost calling it the “Ceasar Building,” referencing a previous owner, was at the top of the tan brick structure.
 The property was last sold in 2024, according to deed records. The city’s assessed value of the property is $686,000.

 8 dead and 19 hurt in building collapse, FDNY says
 By Andy Rose 
 Eight people have died and four are hospitalized in critical condition following the building collapse in Brooklyn, the New York City Fire Department told CNN on Thursday morning.
 Five more victims have serious but non-life-threatening injuries, the agency said.
 Another 10 victims were taken to hospitals with minor injuries.

 8 killed and at least 17 injured in building collapse, mayor says
 By Chris Boyette 
 New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attends a news conference after the building collapse in Brooklyn. 
 Kena Betancur/AFP/Getty Images 
 Eight people are dead and at least 17 injured, including three firefighters, after the collapse Wednesday of a building in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning.
 Facing dangerous conditions, rescue crews worked through the night to find anyone who may still be trapped in the rubble, he said.
 Mamdani is “heartbroken,” and “there are no words for a loss of this magnitude,” he said.

 Death toll climbs to 6 as firefighters search for more people trapped
 The Associated Press
 At least four bodies were pulled from the rubble of the building collapse Thursday morning, New York City’s fire department said, bringing the total death toll to at least six.
 At least 17 people were hospitalized, including four in critical condition.

 Crews are digging through rubble of a collapsed building in New York. Here’s what we know
 By Karina Tsui 
 First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York on Wednesday. 
 Ryan Murphy/AP 
 The mission to search for more victims of a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn continues Thursday, with rescue teams using excavators and buckets to sift through the debris.
 At least six people were killed and 17 more injured, the FDNY told the Associated Press, when a three-story, mixed-use building in the Flatbush neighborhood collapsed into an adjacent construction site at around 4 p.m. Wednesday. Among the victims were at least seven children and a pregnant woman who was pulled out of the structure hours after it came down.
 Rescue workers don’t know how many people may still be trapped, officials said.
 Late Wednesday, rescue teams deployed powerful lights to illuminate the area as they sifted through towering piles of debris. Officials warned the dangerous search for victims could take days .
 New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday said the city’s Department of Buildings would lead the investigation into the collapse, as fire officials were concerned about a secondary structural fall .
 Here’s what else we know:
 Victims unknown: As of Thursday morning, the identifying details of those killed are not known. Among the injured, four people are in critical condition, 12 are stable, and one firefighter had minor injuries, officials said.
 Help center activated: Those impacted by the collapse gathered at a help center at the Flatbush YMCA. Many are “still in shock,” one volunteer said. Flatbush is home to one of the largest, most diverse Caribbean diasporas in the world.
 Mixed-use space: The downed building was built in 1930, city records show. It was a three-story walk-up holding four residential units and a commercial space.
 Digging down: Located at the intersection of Bedford and Flatbush Avenues, the collapsed building stood adjacent to a construction site that was undergoing excavation work at the time of the fall.
 Construction site violations: A demolition contractor in April was issued a violation for unlawfully continuing demolition work at the site. The violation was resolved in October, records show, and the contractor paid $10,000 in penalties.
